name: JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding
question: Can I trust the shape of the output?
summary: Asking for “JSON only” in the prompt still fails some of the time. JSON mode guarantees valid JSON but not your fields. Strict structured outputs go further: the decoder only allows tokens that keep the output valid against your JSON Schema, so the shape is guaranteed within the schema features the provider supports. The shape is not the truth: values can still be wrong, and some constraints, such as numeric ranges, must still be checked in code.
useCases: Any output that feeds code, a database or another tool
Extraction from documents into fixed fields
Tool arguments that must match a schema exactly

steps.title: Define the output as a model
steps.text: A Pydantic model describes the fields and types. The SDK turns it into a JSON Schema for the API.

steps.title: Describe fields, don’t rely on keywords
steps.text: Constraints such as “15 characters” or date formats go in descriptions. Some schema keywords, like lengths and ranges, are not enforced and may be moved into descriptions by the SDK.

steps.title: Let it reason first
steps.text: A reasoning field before the numbers gives the model room to work out totals before committing to them. Very tight formats can otherwise cost accuracy.

steps.title: Parse with the strict mode
steps.text: messages.parse sends the schema through output_config.format; decoding is constrained, so the result always matches the model’s shape.

steps.title: Handle truncation
steps.text: If the response hit max_tokens, the object may be incomplete. Check the stop reason and raise the limit rather than trusting a cut-off answer.

steps.title: Still check the values
steps.text: Every field is present and typed, but a total can still disagree with its items. Business rules are checked next, in the repair loop.

library.name: Anthropic SDK structured outputs
library.what: messages.parse takes a Pydantic model, sends it as a JSON schema through output_config.format, and returns a validated object.

practice.note: Constraints such as lengths and numeric ranges may be moved into descriptions rather than enforced; validate them in code, as in the repair technique.

samples.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class LineItem(BaseModel):
    description: str
    amount_inr: float

class Invoice(BaseModel):
    gstin: str = Field(description="15-character GSTIN of the vendor")
    invoice_no: str
    invoice_date: str = Field(description="ISO date, YYYY-MM-DD")
    items: list[LineItem]
    total_inr: float

client = Anthropic()

def extract(invoice_text: str) -> Invoice:
    r = client.messages.parse(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", max_tokens=1024,
        messages=[{"role": "user",
                   "content": f"Extract the invoice.\n<invoice>{invoice_text}</invoice>"}],
        output_format=Invoice,              # strict JSON schema from the model
    )
    return r.parsed_output                  # an Invoice instance

numericDrill.question: An extractor processes 50,000 invoices a month. With “JSON only” in the prompt, 6% fail to parse and each is retried once at ₹0.40. How much a month do those retries cost?
numericDrill.answer: 6% of 50,000 is 3,000 retries × ₹0.40 = ₹1,200 a month, plus the delay and the retries that fail again. Strict structured outputs remove parse failures entirely, though value checks still apply.

interview.question: What is the difference between JSON mode and strict structured outputs?
interview.answer: JSON mode guarantees syntactically valid JSON but not which fields appear or their types. Strict structured outputs constrain decoding to your JSON Schema, so every required field is present with the right type, within the schema features the provider supports.

interview.question: If the output matches the schema, why validate it again?
interview.answer: A schema guarantees the shape, not the correctness of values. An invoice can have a well-formed total that does not match its items, or a GSTIN that is a string but not a valid one. Some constraints, such as ranges and patterns, may not be enforced by the provider at all, so business rules must be checked in code.
